chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Khattab, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ammar ibn Marwan, from Sama'ah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah bestowed favors upon a people, but they did not show gratitude, so those favors became a burden upon them; and He tested a people with calamities, but they were patient, so those calamities became a favor upon them.
ai.seo_question: How do gratitude and patience determine whether blessings or trials are beneficial or burdensome?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi places this narration within the chapter on earnings (*al-Makasib*), linking material and spiritual states to one's response to divine decree. It underscores the Shia theological principle that the utility of blessings or trials is contingent upon human agency—specifically, whether one exhibits gratitude (*shukr*) or patience (*sabr*)—thereby transforming external circumstances into either a spiritual burden (*wabal*) or a lasting favor (*ni'mah*).
